items.title: 3.3.2 Valence shell electron pair repulsion model (VSEPR)

source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.2, printed pages 52-58 (Table 3.1, Figures 3.9 to 3.20), with Quick Checks 3.5 and 3.6. No 3.3 or 3.3.1 is printed.

blocks.text: The VSEPR model describes the shapes of molecules based on the electron pairs that surround the central atom. This model was presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940. It is based on the assumption that a molecule will take a shape such that the electronic repulsions among the valence electrons of that atom are minimum. In order to have the minimal repulsions, the electron pairs arrange themselves at farthest possible distances. This arrangement of the electron pairs determines the geometry of the resulting molecule.
Postulates:

items: Both the lone pairs (non-bonded) as well as the bond pairs participate in determining the geometries of molecules.
The electron pairs are arranged around the central atom so as to remain at maximum distance apart to avoid repulsions.

The electrons of lone pairs occupy more space than the bond pairs. As a result, the non-bonding electron pairs exert greater repulsive forces on bonding electron pairs and, thus, tend to compress the bond pairs. The magnitude of repulsions between the electron pairs in a given molecule decreases in the following order: Lone pair-lone pair (lp-lp) > lone pair-bond pair (lp-bp) > bond pair-bond pair (bp-bp)
The two electron pairs of a double bond and three electron pairs of a triple bond, contain a higher electronic charge density, but they are regarded as single pairs.
The presence of highly electronegative atoms with the central atom results in decreased electronic repulsions between the bond pairs, but stronger repulsion by the lone pair.

blocks.alt: A strip of two drawings. Left: atom X and atom H with a long, narrow electron cloud stretched between them (a bond pair). Right: atom X with a broad, rounded electron cloud on one side only (a lone pair), visibly fatter than the bond-pair cloud.
blocks.caption: An electron pair shared by two nuclei occupies less space than a lone pair bound by a single nucleus (original drawing after the strip printed above the postulates in the textbook).

blocks.text: Predicting the Shapes of Molecules

In order to illustrate this model, the central atom is named ‘A’. The electron pairs around ‘A’ are designated as ‘B’. There may be different number of electron pairs around the central atom depending upon its valency. It gives rise to various types of molecules, such as AB₂, AB₃, AB₄, etc. The electron pair geometry of a molecule is determined by the total number of electron pairs around ‘A’. Whereas, the actual shape of the molecule is determined by the atoms excluding the lone pairs. Following Table (3.1) gives the possible shapes of different types of molecules having varying numbers of bond and lone pairs.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Table 3.1 puts I₃⁻ with PCl₅ under five electron pairs and no lone pair. The book's own text below (AB₅ type) says the central iodine of I₃⁻ has two bond pairs and three lone pairs: its electron pair geometry is trigonal bipyramidal, but its shape is linear (180°). I₃⁻ belongs in a row with 5 electron pairs and 3 lone pairs.
Steps to Determine the shapes of molecules
The following steps are followed to predict the shape of a molecule.

items: The least electronegative atom or the element with the least number of atoms is mostly selected as the central atom. For example, in CCl₄, the carbon atom is the central atom.

The total number of electron pairs around the central atom are counted (including bond pairs and lone pairs). For example in CCl₄, the total number of bond pairs around the C atom are 4 and it has no lone pair.
The total number of electron pairs determines the electron pair geometry (as in the above table) of the molecule. For example, CCl₄ has total four electron pairs and its geometry is tetrahedral.
Finally, the actual shape of the molecule is determined excluding the lone pairs (if any).

blocks.text: AB₂ type Molecules (Linear geometry)

In such molecules, two electrons pairs around the central atom are arranged at an angle of 180° to minimize repulsions between them. Thus, they form a linear geometry as shown in Figure 3.9. BeCl₂ molecule is of AB₂ type with Be as the central atom and two bond pairs around it, but no lone pair.

blocks.alt: Left: Cl-Be-Cl in a straight line with a curved double arrow over Be labelled 180 degrees. Right: a ball-and-stick model with two large blue Cl balls joined through a small red Be ball in a straight line.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.9: Linear shape of the BeCl2 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.9).

blocks.text: AB₃ type (Trigonal planar geometry)

In AB₃ type molecules, the central atom is surrounded by three electron pairs, which are arranged at maximum distance apart at an angle of 120° giving a trigonal geometry. For example, BF₃ molecule has a trigonal planar shape with each F-B-F bond angle of 120° Figure 3.10. The similar geometries are expected in the hydrides of group 3 (III-A), i.e. AlH₃, GaH₃, BH₃, etc.

blocks.alt: Left: B in the centre bonded to three F atoms, one above and two below, with a curved double arrow between two F atoms labelled 120 degrees. Right: a ball model with a large red B ball and three small blue balls at the corners of a triangle.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.10: BF3 is an AB3 system having triangular planar geometry (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.10).

blocks.text: In SnCl₂, the Sn atom has 4 electrons in its outermost shell. It makes two bonds with two Cl atoms and the remaining two electrons exist as a lone pair (Figure 3.11 below). One of the corners of the triangle is occupied by this lone pair, giving rise to a distorted trigonal electron pair geometry (in vapour phase). The actual shape of SnCl₂ is v-shaped and bond angle less than 120° due to the presence of a lone pair on Sn atom.
AB₃-Type with Multiple Bonds

The molecule of SO₃ has all the three regions occupied by S=O bonds. The structure of SO₃ is perfectly trigonal with each angle equal to 120°. On the other hand, in SO₂, one corner of the triangle is occupied by a lone pair and the other two corners each by a double bond (S=O). Thus, it makes an angular or v-shaped structure just as SnCl₂ does as in Fig 3.12.

blocks.alt: Left: SO3 with S in the centre and three S=O double bonds to O atoms at the corners of a triangle, one angle marked 120 degrees. Right: SO2 with a lone-pair lobe carrying two red dots above S and two S=O bonds below; the O-S-O angle is labelled 'Less than 120 degrees'.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.12: Shapes of multiply bonded SO2 and SO3 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.12).

blocks.text: AB₄ Type (Tetrahedral geometry)

In this type of molecules, the charge clouds due to four electron pairs avoid their electrostatic repulsions by being farthest apart to form the shape of a regular tetrahedron. Each of the bond angles is of 109.5°. For instance, each of the four valence electrons of carbon pair up with the sole electron of a hydrogen atom in methane. The four bonded electron pairs are directed from the center towards the corners of a regular tetrahedron, as following Fig 3.13 with each corner representing a hydrogen nucleus. This arrangement permits a non-planar geometry of electron pairs. Each H-C-H bond angle is perfectly 109.5°. On the same grounds, SiH₄, GeH₄, CCl₄ possess the similar shape.

blocks.alt: Left: a ball-and-stick model of methane, a black C ball joined to four light-blue H balls at the corners of a tetrahedron outlined in blue. Right: a line drawing of CH4 with C bonded to four H atoms, dashed lines joining the H atoms into a tetrahedron, and the H-C-H angle marked 109.5 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.13: Regular tetrahedral shape of the CH4 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.13).

blocks.title: Extend your knowledge
blocks.text: The tetrahedral shape has four corners, four faces, six edges and six bond angles. Ideally it has bond angles of 109.5° each.

In the ammonia molecule (NH₃), there are three atoms attached to the nitrogen atom having one lone pair. Due to a lone pairs the ideal angle 109.5° is reduced to 107° as in Figure 3.14. This effect compels ammonia to assume a triangular pyramidal shape with reduced bond angles, instead of a tetrahedral. The substitution of hydrogen in NH₃ with electronegative atoms like F or Cl further reduces the bond angles. Take the example of NF₃, which contains three highly electronegative F atoms bonded to the N atom. The bond angles are further compressed to 102.5°. The first reason being the strong polarity of N-F bond, due to which N atom pulls the lone pair closer to its nucleus. This, in turn, exerts a stronger repulsion over bonding electrons. Moreover, the bond pairs (N-F bonds) are closer to F atoms than N atom. The increased distances in these bond pairs make their repulsions weaker and allow the bonds to come closer.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of NH3. Left: a tetrahedron with N in the centre, three H balls at three corners and a lone-pair lobe with two dots at the top corner. Middle: a ball model of the pyramidal molecule, N above three H atoms. Right: a wedge-and-dash drawing of N with three H atoms, dashed lines joining the H atoms, and an arrow to the H-N-H angle labelled 107 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.14: Distorted geometry and pyramidal shape of the NH3 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.14).

blocks.text: Experiments reveal that the water molecule (H₂O) is angular or v-shaped, although it has four electron pairs around the central atom. Two of the corners of the tetrahedron are occupied by two lone pairs and the remaining two by bond pairs. But, due to the greater repulsions of the lone pairs, the bond angle is reduced to 104.5° as in Fig 3.15.

blocks.alt: Left, labelled 'Tetrahedral geometry including lone pairs': a red O ball in a tetrahedron with two H balls at the lower corners and two lone-pair lobes, each with two dots, pointing up and down. Right, labelled 'Angular shape of water molecule excluding lone pairs': a bent ball model of H2O and a line drawing H-O-H with the angle marked 104.5 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.15: Water molecule has two lone pairs and is v-shaped with suppressed bond angle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.15).

blocks.text: The VSEPR model also explains the shapes of ions. The hydronium ion [H₃O]⁺ is formed when a water molecule captures a proton. The hydronium ion belongs to AB₄ type with one lone pair and possesses a trigonal pyramidal shape just like the ammonia molecule. The amide ion [NH₂]⁻ is also AB₄ type as it is surrounded by two lone pairs and two bond pairs. Its geometry is tetrahedral, but it has a bent shape (v-shape) similar to the water molecule (Figure 3.16).

blocks.alt: Four parts. 'Hydronium ion': a water molecule with red lone-pair electrons, a curved arrow from a lone pair to H+, and an arrow down to the H3O+ Lewis structure with one lone pair and a + charge. 'Tetrahedral electron pair geometry': O in a tetrahedron with three H balls and a lone-pair lobe at the top. 'Trigonal pyramidal shape': O ball above three H balls. 'V-shaped amide ion': N with two green lone-pair lobes and two bonds to H at 104.1 degrees, in square brackets with a minus charge.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.16: Shapes of hydronium (H3O+) and amide ions (NH2-) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.16).

blocks.title: Quick Check 3.5
blocks.text:
a) Calculate the number of bond pairs and lone pairs in SiH₄, H₂Se, and PH₃.
b) Predict the shapes and angles in SiH₄, H₂Se, and PH₃.
c) Predict how the bond angle in H₂S would be different from that in H₂O.
AB₅ type (Trigonal Bipyramid Geometry)

In AB₅ type molecules, repulsions between the five electron pairs can be minimized by an even distribution of electrons among the corners of a trigonal bipyramid. In a trigonal bipyramid, three positions lie along the corners of the planar triangle, whereas, the other two positions lie along an axis perpendicular to the plane. This is evident from the geometry of the PCl₅ molecule given in Figure 3.17. The angles within the plane are 120° and that between the axial atom and a planar atom is 90°.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of PCl5. Left: the Lewis structure, P bonded to five Cl atoms, each Cl with three lone pairs. Middle: five grey electron-pair lobes around a red P ball inside a dotted trigonal bipyramid. Right: a ball-and-stick model with a red P ball and five green Cl balls, two on the vertical axis and three around the middle.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.17: Lewis structure and shape of PCl5 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.17).

blocks.text: Just as in the AB₃ and AB₄ types, the presence of lone pairs in AB₅ system also changes the shape and the angles, but the change in this case is more dramatic. Tri-iodide ion [I₃]⁻ is linear, although it is an AB₅ system. The central atom in this ion is the iodine atom. There are five electron pairs around the iodine atom including two bond pairs and three lone pairs. Therefore, it is an AB₅ type molecule with three lone pairs and possesses trigonal bipyramidal geometry. The lone pairs occupy the corners of the trigonal region and the iodine atoms occur on the apices, one being above and the second below the plane. However, excluding the three lone pairs, the actual shape of the tri-iodide ion is linear and the iodine atoms are farthest apart at an angle of 180° as in Figure 3.18.

blocks.alt: A red central iodine ball with two iodine balls straight above and below it on a vertical rod, and three grey lone-pair lobes around the middle, one to the left and two to the right. A semicircular arc on the left joins the top and bottom iodine atoms and is labelled 180 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.18: Shape of tri-iodide ion ([I3]-) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.18).

blocks.text: AB₆ type molecules (Octahedral Geometry)

AB₆ type molecules have 6 electron pairs around the central atom. The repulsions between the electron pairs can be minimized by assuming an octahedral geometry. In this geometry, four electron pairs are at the corners of a planar square and the other two lie along an axis perpendicular to the square. All the ABA angles in this type of geometry are of 90°. The Lewis structure of SF₆ is given in Figure 3.19, it shows that this is an AB₆ type molecule.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of SF6. Left: the Lewis structure, S bonded to six F atoms, each F with three lone pairs. Middle: an octahedral ball-and-stick model, a yellow S ball joined to six green F balls with dashed octahedron edges. Right: a wedge-and-dash drawing with F above and below S, two hashed bonds behind and two wedged bonds in front, and two angles marked 90 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.19: Lewis structure and octahedral shape of SF6 with each angle of 90 degrees (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.19).

blocks.text: XeF₄ is an AB₆ type molecule with four bond pairs and two lone pairs. The two lone pairs remain at farthest distance at angle of 180°. Excluding the lone pairs, the actual shape of XeF₄ is square planar with all F-P-F angles equal to 90°.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: XeF₄ has no phosphorus atom. The angles of the square planar molecule are the F-Xe-F angles, each 90°.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of XeF4. Left: the Lewis structure, Xe with two lone pairs bonded to four F atoms, each F with three lone pairs. Middle: an orange Xe ball with four green F balls around it and two blue lone-pair lobes pointing up and down, with an arc and the label 'lone pair is farthest at 180 degrees'. Right: a square planar ball model, Xe in the centre of a dashed square of four F atoms, with one angle marked 90 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.20: Lewis structure and square planar shape of XeF4 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.20).
